title: AI handwriting analysis divides the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaa) into two groups of columns, which its authors attribute to two scribes; researchers in Norway question the method in 2025
summary: Groningen's AI writer-identification method split the Great Isaiah Scroll's 54 columns into two groups, which its authors attribute to two scribes; researchers in Norway questioned it in 2025.
account: On 21 April 2021 Mladen Popović, Maruf Dhali and Lambert Schomaker of the University of Groningen published an artificial-intelligence analysis in PLOS ONE. It examined the handwriting of the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaa) from the Dead Sea Scrolls. They used pattern recognition on digitized images of the scroll's 54 columns. The columns fell into two statistically distinct groups, with a transition in columns 27–29. They concluded that two main scribes with different writing patterns were responsible for the scroll. Most scholars had argued or assumed that one scribe copied the whole manuscript. Some earlier scholars had suggested a change after column 27 on other grounds, and the AI analysis supplied quantitative evidence. The authors note that a change of pen or writing conditions could contribute to the difference. The same team developed the method and wrote the finding, and acceptance rests on the journal's peer review. The same day Peter Phillips of Durham University wrote in The Conversation that a change of scribe is the most likely conclusion. In June 2025 Tabita Tobing and Patrick Bours of the Norwegian University of Science and Technology retraced a column-based method on the same images. They argue that the 2021 analysis was framed to validate a two-scribe hypothesis. They found that the two-scribe split separates letters better than other groupings, with only moderate scores. They judge that hinge features alone cannot attribute scribes reliably.
purpose: Writer identification in ancient manuscripts to distinguish individual scribes
system: Groningen AI-based writer-identification pipeline (neural-network binarisation with textural and allographic feature analysis)
segment: Palaeography of the Dead Sea Scrolls

ai_role.statement: The AI analysis produced the statistical separation of the columns into two groups. The authors made the scribal interpretation and concluded that two scribes were responsible. The method's developers and the finding's authors are the same team. The authors note that a change of pen or writing conditions could contribute to the difference, and Peter Phillips of Durham University judges a change of scribe the most likely explanation. A 2025 retest by Tobing and Bours finds that hinge features alone give only moderate separation.

fields.account: On 21 April 2021 Mladen Popović, Maruf Dhali and Lambert Schomaker of the University of Groningen published an artificial-intelligence analysis in PLOS ONE. It examined the handwriting of the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaa) from the Dead Sea Scrolls. They used pattern recognition on digitized images of the scroll's 54 columns. The columns fell into two statistically distinct groups, with a transition in columns 27–29. They concluded that two main scribes with different writing patterns were responsible for the scroll. Most scholars had argued or assumed that one scribe copied the whole manuscript. Some earlier scholars had suggested a change after column 27 on other grounds, and the AI analysis supplied quantitative evidence. The authors note that a change of pen or writing conditions could contribute to the difference. The same team developed the method and wrote the finding, and acceptance rests on the journal's peer review. The same day Peter Phillips of Durham University wrote in The Conversation that a change of scribe is the most likely conclusion. In June 2025 Tabita Tobing and Patrick Bours of the Norwegian University of Science and Technology retraced a column-based method on the same images. They argue that the 2021 analysis was framed to validate a two-scribe hypothesis. They found that the two-scribe split separates letters better than other groupings, with only moderate scores. They judge that hinge features alone cannot attribute scribes reliably.
